newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: U.S. envoy Solarz seeks Cambodia solution with ASE.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy Solarz seeks Cambodia solution with ASE.

text.p: President Clinton's special envoy on Cambodia said on Wednesday he wants to work with the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) on a solution to Cambodia's troubles.

"We very much want to work with our friends in ASEAN and other countries in region," former U.S. congressman Stephen Solarz told reporters after meeting Malaysian Foreign minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi.

"We think the best chance of achieving an acceptable resolution of the Cambodian crisis is if we can find a way to work together," said Solarz who is on an Asian diplomatic shuttle seeking a solution to the turmoil.

Cambodia was to have joined ASEAN at a special ceremony on Wednesday along with Burma and Laos. But after Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's bloody overthrow of First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh earlier this month, ASEAN postponed Cambodia's admission indefinitely.
Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot was to arrive around midday on Wednesday determined to make a last-ditch effort to get into the grouping.
He has written a letter to the ASEAN foreign ministers asking the group to go ahead with Cambodia's admission this week, Abdullah said on Tuesday.
ASEAN is holding its annual foreign ministers' meeting in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday and Friday.
The ministers were to decide later on Wednesday what to do about Cambodia, which is still an observer in the group.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas was to give a report to the ministers later on Wednesday on an ASEAN mediation effort that he headed last week.
Hun Sen has emphatically rejected ASEAN's offer to mediate the dispute between him and Ranariddh, saying foreigners should stay out of Cambodia's business.
The United States and Germany have suspended their aid programmes to Cambodia in response to Ranariddh's overthrow.
At least half of Cambodia's national budget is funded by foreign aid, which has in any case ground to a halt with the evacuation of many of the foreigners running the programmes.

Solarz said the international community which brokered the 1991 Paris Peace Accords, which paved the way for elections and the resulting unwieldy coalition government of Hun Sen and Ranariddh, had a vital stake in Cambodia.
"I think it's clear that everyone believes the Paris agreement should be respected and upheld and the challenge is how to find a way to do that," Solarz said.
Solarz was scheduled to meet Alatas and other foreign ministers later on Wednesday. He is due to fly to Bangkok and then to Phnom Penh on Thursday for meetings with Ranariddh and Hun Sen.
